item.title: Large-deformation constitutive modeling of viscoelastic foams: Application to an open-cell foam material
item.description: arXiv:2611.33416v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Open-cell elastomeric foams are widely utilized for impact protection and cushioning applications. These foams can demonstrate remarkable elastic compressibility and rate sensitivity over a wide range of force and acceleration protection levels. They often exhibit volumetric-distortional coupling in their mechanical response and potentially compaction banding when subjected to dynamic loads. Here, a phenomenological modeling framework, adopted previously for closed-cell foams, is specified using an experimental characterization-based approach for calibrating and validating the large-deformation, viscoelastic material model. Homogeneous simple compression and tension experiments were performed on isotropic, open-cell viscoelastic foam materials, and stress-strain and lateral-axial strain data were used for model calibration. Data were collected at decadal strain rates to inform the rate-sensitive aspects of the model. The modeling approach involved decomposing the total material response into an equilibrium hyperelastic contribution and several nonlinear, Maxwell-like contributions and utilized invariants of the logarithmic strain to account for large deformations and the strong volumetric-distortional coupling effect. A new strain localization detection algorithm was developed and used to check for the formation of compaction bands, which would invalidate modeling assumptions for the calibration experiments. To validate the predictive capability of the constitutive model, experiments were conducted that involved intentionally inhomogeneous deformations over a spectrum of strain rates and deformation types. The consistency between the measured responses from the validation experiments and the model predictions obtained from finite-element-based numerical simulations was largely within the experimental uncertainty bounds, demonstrating the predictive capability of the model.

item.title: Dancing dervishes, spinning skirts and whirling waves
item.description: arXiv:2611.33429v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Inspired by the patterns seen in the tunic of a whirling dervish or the long skirt of a Kathak dancer, we study the dynamics of a \emph{soft} heavy circular sheet spinning steadily around its axis. Using experiments, we show that the initially draped sheet can pass through three archetypal states as it rotates: a gravity-dominated draped rotation state, a flat state, and finally a whirling state marked by retrograde rotation of wavy patterns relative to the rotating frame. We map out these various configurations in a three-dimensional phase diagram, analyze the transitions using a minimal model, and derive scaling laws to describe the phase boundaries which we confirm using experiments.
item.dc:creator: Paul R. Kaneelil, Sifan Yin, L. Mahadevan

item.title: Soft Matter, Hard Rules: Emulsions Follow the Laws of Granular Suspension Rheology
item.description: arXiv:2611.33526v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The flow of dense emulsions underlies applications from food and pharmaceutical processing to bioengineering, yet their rheology remains difficult to interpret under conventional volume-imposed conditions. Here, we change the control variable to osmotic-pressure using a recently developed instrument -- the Capillarytron. This approach reveals a unified rheological structure where the osmotic pressure $\Pi$, by controlling droplet deformation, sets a pressure-dependent jamming volume fraction. When expressed in terms of the distance to this jamming point, all rheological data -- spanning both $\Pi$- and $\phi$-imposed measurements -- collapse onto a single power-law divergence, akin to granular suspensions. The resulting constitutive relations provide a predictive, parameter-free description of emulsion rheology across Newtonian, yielding, and shear-thinning regimes. Together with recent results on soft spheres, our findings point to a unifying paradigm: Soft amorphous materials -- from soft spheres to emulsions and likely foams -- obey the same hard rules as granular suspensions, with softness entering through a pressure-dependent jamming point. This framework rationalizes Herschel-Bulkley rheology, assigns its parameters microscopic meaning, and opens perspectives on rigidity transitions in soft, deformable systems, including biological tissues.
item.dc:creator: Wenjun Chen, Eric De Giuli, Matthieu Wyart, Yo\"el Forterre, Jasna Bruji\'c, Bloen Metzger

item.title: Frustration in system with intercalated and bilayer smectic structure
item.description: arXiv:2611.34072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The dimeric mesogens exhibit an unusual variety of mesophases - nematic and smectic, with distinctly different packing schemes. The relation between molecular and mesophase structure was studied for homologue series of non-symmetric bent dimers CBO6.Om, obtained by serial Pd- and Pt-catalyzed cross-coupling chemical reactions. The shorter homologues of the series form smectics with an intercalated structure, and longer homologues form bilayer smectics with broken up-down symmetry of molecular orientation within the layers, for intermediate homologues frustration leads to a nematic gap. The additional structure complexity arises from the tendency of bent dimers to form twisted structures, in which the azimuthal angle of tilted molecules forms both short- and long-pitch helices. Here we confirm, through resonant X-ray diffraction, that longer homologues form a helical four-layer structure of SmCTB-SH phase, along with a more complex one in which, in addition to the basic four-layer unit, an extra helix is superimposed, SmCTB-DH phase. This additional helix has a periodicity that is strongly temperature-dependent; upon cooling, it changes from 100 nm to 40 nm.
item.dc:creator: Calum J. Gibb, Claudio Flores Fernandez, Magdalena M. Majewska, John M. D. Storey, Corrie T. Imrie, Ewa Gorecka, Damian Pociecha

item.title: Length-scales and fractal scaling in dairy gels: comparisons of the insights from ultra-small angle neutron scattering and rheology
item.description: arXiv:2611.34194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A key structural parameter that dictates the textural properties of a particulate gel is the fractal dimension (Df) of the network indicating self-similarity within the spatial range defined by the correlation length (xi). In this study dairy gels are formed from reconstituted skim milk at defined CM volume fractions via two different mechanisms: acidification, and enzymatic (rennet)-induction. Oscillatory rheology is performed to obtain the gelation times, the time-scale for the maturation of mechanical properties of the gel, and the viscoelastic properties of the gel. A direct probe of gel structure is ultra-small-angle neutron scattering (USANS) examining length-scales from approximately 60 nm up to 15 microns. Structural information is extracted from USANS of matured gels by comparing the measured differential scattering cross-section with that calculated from a model constrained by the sample composition. Time-scales for structural equilibration from USANS perspective were shorter than the rheological gelation time for both gels. Rheological scaling theories are utilized to relate the microstructure to their bulk mechanical properties. We show that the fractal scaling at low-q (scattering vectors), due to aggregation of CM, extracted from the USANS at the longest timescales is described by a power-law density-density correlation function, and that rheology relates - through Shih-Wu-Morbidelli models - the local elasticity both within and between the fractal flocs formed by these particles over different size ranges to the bulk moduli of the gels. There are similar values of fractal dimensions from both techniques but different sizes attributed to the complex fractal evolution during dairy gelation, which leaves space to refinements of the models.
item.dc:creator: Koduvayur A. Ramya, Liliana de Campo, Markus Strobl, Fran\c{c}ois Bou\'e, Christopher J. Garvey

item.title: Collective relaxation dynamics and vitrification in hexatic smectic binary equimolar mixtures containing component with varying C$_3$F$_7$CH$_2$OC$_m$H$_{2m}$- chain length
item.description: arXiv:2611.34286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Differential scanning calorimetry, polarizing optical microscopy, and broadband dielectric spectroscopy are applied for investigation of phase transitions in equimolar binary mixtures consisting of the MHPOBC liquid crystal as one component and 3FmHPhH6 homologs as a second component with different C$_3$F$_7$CH$_2$OC$_m$H$_{2m}$- chain length (m = 2-7). The paraelectric smectic A* - ferroelectric smectic C* - antiferroelectric smectic C$_A$* - hexatic smectic X$_A$* - glassy smectic X$_A$* sequence is observed for all mixtures. The appearance of the bond-orientational order in smectic X$_A$* is accompanied by an additional relaxation process P$_{hex}$ in dielectric spectra at the low-frequency side of the P$_H$ phason, consistent with its assignment to bond-orientational fluctuations. The empirical exponential-power relationship is proposed for the ratio between the relaxation times of P$_{hex}$ and P$_H$. The behavior of the structural $\alpha$-relaxation and secondary $\beta$-relaxation in smectic X$_A$* depends on the m parameter, changing from overlapping $\alpha$ and $\beta$ processes for m = 2 to well-separated for m = 6, 7. A double glass transition is observed by calorimetry on heating for m = 5-7. The calorimetric glass transition temperature shows a composition-dependent correspondence with temperatures at which either the P$_H$ or $\alpha$-relaxation time reaches 100 s, suggesting that different relaxation processes may contribute to vitrification.
item.dc:creator: Aleksandra Deptuch, Mateusz P\k{a}czek, Anna Drzewicz, Marcin Piwowarczyk, Magdalena Urba\'nska, Ewa Juszy\'nska-Ga{\l}\k{a}zka

item.title: A Thermodynamically Consistent Model of a Rechargeable Salt-in-Polyelectrolyte Battery
item.description: arXiv:2611.34415v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present an isothermal, thermodynamically consistent model of a salt-in-polyelectrolyte battery with intercalation and deintercalation reactions of cations occurring at the electrode-electrolyte interfaces under galvanostatic conditions. For the electrolyte, we consider polyelectrolytes, which are polyanions, with neutralizing cations (i.e., counterions) such as lithium, along with a monovalent salt containing the same cations. Models of batteries containing either a dual-ion-conductor (DIC) electrolyte (i.e., uncharged polymers with added salt) or a single-ion-conductor (SIC) electrolyte (i.e., charged polymers without added salt) emerge as limiting cases of this thermodynamically consistent model. Once the model is presented in its most general context, we make specific choices so that it captures well-known mechanisms. In particular, the governing diffusion equations recover Fick's law of diffusion, and the cation-transfer reaction rate is described by the Butler--Volmer equation. The DIC and SIC limiting cases provide a framework for comparing the corresponding batteries. One-dimensional DIC and SIC charge--discharge simulations at matched current and duration illustrate concentration redistribution, polarization, and electrode utilization. Numerical accuracy checks quantify sensitivity to discretization; distinct initial inventories qualify the comparison.
item.dc:creator: Charlotte Beckford, Rajeev Kumar, Steven M. Wise

item.title: Anomalous scaling of coalescence in a Hele-Shaw cell
item.description: arXiv:2611.33348v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We investigate the merging of two drops between two narrowly spaced plates, a so-called Hele-Shaw cell. For this, we solve the Hele-Shaw equations in two dimensions, driven by surface tension, focusing on early times after initial reconnection. Combining numerical simulations with theory, we show that the coalescence dynamics are self-similar at early times, with the size of the contact region between the drops growing as $t^{3/13}$. We find this power law using a matched asymptotic analysis, which reveals a complex geometry consisting of a small bubble that gets entrained between the drops as they come together. These predictions match perfectly to our simulations, and agree with the most recent experimental data.
item.dc:creator: Luke Neville, Rodolfo Brand\~ao, Marco A. Fontelos, Jens Eggers

item.title: Systematic study of the performance of small robots on controlled laboratory substrates
item.description: arXiv:2611.33702v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The design of robots able to locomote effectively over a diversity of terrain requires detailed ground interaction models; unfortunately such models are lacking due to the complicated response of real world substrates which can yield and flow in response to loading. To advance our understanding of the relevant modeling and design issues, we conduct a comparative study of the performance of DASH and RoACH, two small, biologically inspired, six legged, lightweight (10 cm, 20 g) robots fabricated using the smart composite microstructure (SCM) process. We systematically examine performance of both robots on rigid and flowing substrates. Varying both ground properties and limb stride frequency, we investigate average speed, mean mechanical power and cost of transport, and stability. We find that robot performance and stability is sensitive to the physics of ground interaction: on hard ground kinetic energy must be managed to prevent yaw, pitch, and roll instability to maintain high performance, while on sand the fluidizing interaction leads to increased cost of transport and lower running speeds. We also observe that the characteristic limb morphology and kinematics of each robot result in distinct differences in their abilities to traverse different terrains. Our systematic studies are the first step toward developing models of interaction of limbs with complex terrain as well as developing improved limb morphologies and control strategies.
item.dc:creator: Chen Li, Aaron M. Hoover, Paul Birkmeyer, Paul B. Umbanhowar, Ronald S. Fearing, Daniel I. Goldman

item.title: Exclusion and internal structure in the association/dissociation kinetics of DNA-binding proteins in the fast diffusion limit
item.description: arXiv:2611.33740v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In many canonical biophysical and biochemical contexts, complex diffusing DNA-binding proteins undergoing nonspecific adsorption and desorption can exist in different conformational states. Equilibrium binding theories and kinetic models of competing ligands provide a basis for describing these systems. Coupling the internal conformational kinetics of bound proteins to exclusion and diffusion requires tracking both protein positions and binding states. Closed-form, tractable mathematical models that accurately describe the stochastic dynamics of structured proteins that bind to and diffuse along DNA are lacking. Here, we develop a new coarse-grained stochastic model of nonspecific DNA-protein binding in the fast diffusion regime, from which we derive an effective Markov model and its corresponding mean-field approximation that incorporates protein footprint size and conformational switching. We fit our new model quantitatively to previously measured dynamics of Replication Protein A (RPA) binding to ssDNA. Finally, by including multisegment binding states, our analysis captures facilitated exchange, revealing how multisegment architecture balances high affinity with rapid remodeling. Our theoretical model applies broadly to many other DNA-binding protein systems, including nucleosomes, ssDNA-binding proteins, and other multisegment complexes, providing accurate predictions and new strategies for evaluating experimental data.
item.dc:creator: Xiangting Li, Tom Chou

item.title: Exploring Physical Mechanisms Underlying the Emergence of Collective Order
item.description: arXiv:2611.33988v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emergence of collective order from disordered constituents is a hallmark of active matter, and the Vicsek model (VM) serves as a paradigmatic system for its study. However, whether density-induced emergence in the VM differs between angular (intrinsic) and vectorial (extrinsic) noise, and what mechanisms govern the transitions, remain largely unexplored. Remarkably, we uncover that collective order emerges from a disordered state in a continuous-like manner under intrinsic noise but abruptly under extrinsic noise. Combining nonequilibrium landscape-flux theory with a coarse-grained mapping method, we show that the landscape evolves continuously from a single basin to two and back to one under intrinsic noise, but the two-basin landscape appears abruptly under extrinsic noise across the critical transition to flocking. The counterclockwise nonequilibrium flux sustains global circular motion, providing the driving force for reshaping the landscape. The mean flux and entropy production rate change steeply near the emergence threshold and exhibit pronounced peaks within the coexistence region, identifying them as the dynamical and thermodynamic origins of emergence. Our findings reveal a distinct abrupt emergence under extrinsic noise and offer deeper mechanistic insight, practical applications (e.g., locating phase boundaries and distinguishing transition types), and extensibility to other nonequilibrium collective systems.
item.dc:creator: Yitong Cai, Ruizhe Yan, Dongrun Jian, Jie Su, Jin Wang

item.title: Discotic columnar phase in a three-dimensional monomer-tetramer model of Heilmann and Lieb with side-to-side attraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.34796v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Model III of Heilmann--Lieb (1979), a lattice model for liquid crystals consisting of tetramers (plaquettes) on the cubic lattice at chemical potential $\mu$, interacting via a hard-core repulsion and a lateral attraction of strength $a>0$ between coplanar, aligned tetramers. The model was conjectured to exhibit liquid-crystalline order at low temperature provided that $\mu+2a>0$. We establish discotic columnar order throughout this regime, fully resolving the conjecture. Specifically, we prove the existence of exactly twelve extremal and periodic Gibbs measures, each breaking rotational symmetry, with one of three tetramer orientations dominant, and translational symmetry in exactly two directions, with one of four tetramer parities dominant within that orientation. Thus, the tetramers form one-dimensional columns arranged on a square lattice. This arrangement is not a priori evident from the zero-temperature picture, where energy only enforces a layered structure: each layer is fully packed and crystalline, but different layers are free to shift independently within their planes. The main novelty here lies in showing how thermal fluctuations lift this degeneracy in favor of the twelve ground states in which all tetramers share a common parity.
item.dc:creator: Qidong He

item.title: Covariant Onsager and Onsager-Machlup principles for active and inertial dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2604.22371v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Onsager principle provides a variational route to the phenomenological equations of dissipative dynamics through the minimization of the Rayleighian. We develop a covariant formulation of the Onsager principle for active and inertial systems, ensuring geometric consistency under coordinate transformations. To further incorporate thermal fluctuations, we formulate the Onsager-Machlup principle for active and inertial systems by considering the Onsager-Machlup functional and the corresponding path probability for stochastic trajectories. Requiring that the path probability obeys the detailed fluctuation theorem, we show that the extended Onsager-Machlup theory is consistent with stochastic thermodynamics. The extended OP and OMP offer a unified and useful variational framework for deriving the dynamical equations of active and inertial systems.
item.dc:creator: Kento Yasuda, Bin Zheng, Zhongqiang Xiong, Zhanglin Hou, Kenta Ishimoto, Xinpeng Xu, David Andelman, Shigeyuki Komura

item.title: Variational approach to droplet motion on uneven solid surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation
item.description: arXiv:2605.12393v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We show how dynamical equations for liquid films and drops on uneven surfaces, including contact line dynamics and evaporation/condensation effects, may be formulated as a variational dynamics, generated via Onsager's variational principle. The theory applies in the isothermal overdamped-dynamics limit. We apply this general approach to obtain several well-known results on contact line dynamics and to study drops pinning and sliding on inclined corrugated surfaces. This approach constructs the dynamical equations starting from the free energy of the system and therefore has the advantage that it naturally incorporates the correct equilibrium properties.
item.dc:creator: Gyula I T\'oth, David N Sibley, Agnes J Bok\'anyi-T\'oth, Dmitri Tseluiko, Andrew J Archer

item.title: A method for measuring the dispersion of elastic waves in disordered computer-solids
item.description: arXiv:2607.11395v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The dispersion of elastic waves in disordered solids plays a key role in determining the vibrational density of states and harmonic wave attenuation rates. As such, the availability of robust computational approaches to the precise extraction of the dispersion is of key importance. Here we present a simple method -- the imposed wave method (IWM) -- , which provides direct access to the dispersion of elastic waves in computer models of solids, without any fitting involved. We directly benchmark the method against the `ground-truth' obtained from direct diagonalization of solids' hessian matrices, to find good agreement. We discuss limitations of and finite-size effects in the method, and show that exploiting the method's finite-size scaling provides access to a fundamental quantifier of mechanical disorder that determines wave attenuation rates and spectral widths.
item.dc:creator: Edan Lerner

item.title: Emergent odd response in active chiral films
item.description: arXiv:2607.17717v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Active chiral fluids can support an anomalous transport coefficient known as odd (or Hall) viscosity. Hydrodynamic descriptions of such fluids typically introduce odd viscosity phenomenologically. How such a response emerges from specific microscopic interactions remains incompletely understood. Here, building on classical shear rheology, we microscopically derive an odd rheological response in active chiral films: thin layers of torque-exerting, elongated particles anchored to a no-slip surface. A canonical realization of such a film is the bacterial carpet, in which flagellated bacteria are tethered head-down to a solid surface while their flagella remain free to spin and inject angular momentum into the surrounding fluid. Using a Smoluchowski kinetic theory for the orientational dynamics of these anchored particles, we derive their stress response to an imposed shear flow. We reveal that shear-induced reorientation leads to a flow-aligned polarization and a transverse surface traction from which the odd-viscosity tensor follows in closed form. This approach stands in contrast with existing microscopic theories, in which the axis of torque injection is insensitive to the flow rather than set by it. Numerical solutions of the kinetic theory further highlight saturation of the transverse traction at strong shear, driven by this orientation dynamics -- signaling departure from linear response. Our results demonstrate how odd viscosity can emerge self-consistently as a coarse-grained rheological signature of active fluid-structure interaction and establish active chiral films as a new controllable setting for odd hydrodynamics.
item.dc:creator: Seema Chahal, D. Naveen Kumar, Brato Chakrabarti

item.title: Morphogenic necking of surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.31360v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Surface morphogenesis occurs across biological scales, from subcellular vesicles and cells to visceral organs, tissue organoids, and whole organisms. Since morphogenesis often involves changes in topology, a natural question is that of appropriate mathematical descriptions that provide an approach to topological transitions of thin surfaces. Here, we suggest a general intrinsic framework coupling morphogen organization to surface geometry. We propose a minimal geometric model in which smoothing competes with morphogen-induced deformation to regulate shape, while loss of this balance can bring a surface toward a topological transition via neck constriction. A simple dynamical model coupling a scalar field to the surface metric reveals two mechanisms: gradient-driven constriction at steep morphogen transitions and curvature-driven constriction near localized morphogen peaks. For frozen morphogen profiles in simple axisymmetric examples, the gradient-driven route gives exact algebraic contraction, while the curvature-driven route gives local exponential contraction.
item.dc:creator: Farzan Vafa, Puskar Mondal, L. Mahadevan

item.title: Snap-Through Symmetry Breaking in Multicellular Aggregates
item.description: arXiv:2611.32832v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Symmetry breaking is a fundamental process in biological organization. Yet the physical mechanisms that control its onset in multicellular systems remain poorly understood. Motivated by gastruloids -- multicellular aggregates in which cells differentiate and spontaneously break symmetry -- we study a two-phase viscoelastic solid drop as a minimal model of tissue polarization. We show that elastocapillary competition fundamentally alters the classical engulfing transition of fluid drops. While symmetry breaking occurs continuously in the purely viscous limit, bulk elasticity instead leads to a discontinuous snap-like transition. We demonstrate that this behavior can be understood as a wetting transition governed by a spreading coefficient which depends on the drop size and phase volume fraction. Applying our model to gastruloids, we find a critical volume fraction for symmetry breaking, providing a self-organized mechanism for robust developmental timing. Our results identify a generic elastocapillary transition that enables spontaneous symmetry breaking in biphasic drops.
item.dc:creator: Mart\'i Planasdemunt-Hospital, David Oriola

item.title: Renormalization for Robust Memory without Synchronization
item.description: arXiv:2610.40651v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Local error correction can preserve classical information against noise, but protection under synchronized updates need not survive when sites evolve at independent random times. Establishing stability is particularly challenging when protection relies on the collective action of competing local rules. Here we develop a spacetime renormalization framework that reveals how independently acting local updates can collectively stabilize memory. We identify sufficient conditions under which the geometry of stable interfaces and suppression of defect propagation produce reliable erosion at large scales. Applying this framework, we prove the stability of the asynchronous R squeezing code and introduce robust processes in two and three dimensions. In these systems, both encoded phases persist under sufficiently weak noise, even when the noise favors one phase. Our results provide a criterion for designing autonomous memories sustained by competing local stochastic dynamics.
item.dc:creator: Shashwat Chakraborty, Jong Yeon Lee

item.title: From Growth Inhibition to Fluctuations: Testing an Ising Model of Bacterial Responses to Antibiotics
item.description: arXiv:2611.31609v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Complex networks of biochemical reactions have been proposed to exhibit emergent cooperativity that can be described by an effective Ising model, with a small number of parameters encoding collective interactions. Here this mapping is experimentally tested using the response of three bacterial species to a range of antibiotics acting on different cellular targets. The Ising description is compared to the conventional Hill model, examining both the mean growth-rate response and, importantly, its population growth-rate heterogeneity (PGRH). While both models describe the mean growth-rate dependence on antibiotic concentration comparably well, we find that the Ising model provides a markedly better description of PGRH, offering an additional and more stringent test of the collective description. The fitted Ising interaction strength is systematically related to the Hill exponent and increases with the functional distance of the antibiotic target from the protein-production machinery. These results provide experimental support for describing complex biochemical reaction networks through effective cooperative Ising interactions, and suggest that the collective response of bacterial growth to antibiotics reflects the organization of the underlying metabolic network.
item.dc:creator: Pietro Cicuta, Morten Kals, Nir S. Gov
